pos: n. (Anton Koberger, c. 1440–1513, printer of Nuremberg)
etymology: Latin Antonius, a Roman family name; German Koberger, from a Franconian place-name.
biblical_def: Anton Koberger ran the largest printing house in Europe before the Reformation began: twenty-four presses at Nuremberg, a hundred workmen, agents from Paris to Venice to Budapest. He printed something over two hundred titles, among them fifteen editions of the Latin Bible, the ninth German Bible of 1483, and the great illustrated world chronicle of 1493. He died four years before the theses were posted, and he belongs in this account for exactly that reason: the machine that carried the Reformation across Germany in eighteen months had been built, staffed and supplied by Catholic printers for a Catholic market, and it was waiting. Luther did not invent the press or the distribution network or the reading public. He wrote in German, at length, in a hurry, and the trade did the rest. There is a providence in the sequence that neither side planned and neither side could have stopped. “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done” (Isa 46:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines press as a machine for printing, and typography as the art of printing.
webster_full: PRESS, n. A machine for printing; called a printing-press.
TY'POGRAPHY, n. The art of printing; the operation of impressing letters and words on forms.
FO'LIO, n. A book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet of paper.
A'GENT, n. A factor; a substitute or deputy, appointed to transact business for another.
scriptures: Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
Dan 4:35

And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?
Eph 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
corruption_summary: Twenty-four presses at Nuremberg, built for one market and waiting for another.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the account of the Reformation as a triumph of technology, in which a new machine made an old church indefensible and the doctrine is incidental to the mechanism. The mechanism was real and Koberger built a great deal of it. It had been running for sixty years, almost entirely in the service of the church it would help to break, and it did not produce a Reformation in all that time.

The principle to recover is that God governs the means as well as the end, and arranges both long before the men involved can see the pattern. “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10). Nebuchadnezzar learned the same lesson in a harder school: “none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?” (Dan 4:35). Paul gives the comprehensive form: God “worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Eph 1:11).

pos: n. (Johann Froben, c. 1460–1527, printer of Basel)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Froben, from Old High German, wise and glad.
biblical_def: Johann Froben made Basel the scholarly printing capital of northern Europe and was Erasmus's printer and friend; Erasmus lived in his house for years and died in Basel largely because Froben's press was there. In 1516 Froben printed the Greek New Testament Erasmus had edited, the first published Greek text of the New Testament, with a fresh Latin version beside it. The edition was rushed and the Greek has real faults; it is also the text from which Luther translated into German at the Wartburg and Tyndale into English at Worms, and the ancestor of the printed Greek tradition that carried the Reformation. Froben also printed the fathers in good editions, Jerome and Augustine among them, and he employed Holbein to decorate his books. He was not a partisan and refused to print the Lutheran polemic; he printed scholarship and left the conclusions to the reader. The Greek New Testament he set in a hurry in 1516 did more than any pamphlet he declined. “unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines edition as the publication of a book, and collation as a comparison of one copy with another.
webster_full: EDI'TION, n. The publication of any book; also, the whole number of copies published at once.
COLLA'TION, n. A comparison of one copy or thing of a like kind with another.
AP'PARATUS, n. Things provided as means to some end; a complete set of instruments or utensils.
GREEK, n. A native of Greece; the language of Greece.
scriptures: Rom 3:2
Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.
If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;

The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Basel's great press, Erasmus's house, and the Greek New Testament of 1516.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the habit of treating the 1516 Greek New Testament as either beyond criticism or as discredited, when the honest account is simply that it was a first attempt made in haste from a handful of late manuscripts, with real errors in it, which nonetheless put the Greek text into the hands of every scholar in Europe for the first time since the fall of Constantinople.

The principle to recover is that the oracles were given in particular languages and that the church is therefore permanently dependent on the preservation and circulation of those texts. “unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2). The Lord's own estimate of the written word's durability is absolute: “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35). And the claim made for the whole of it covers its profit as well as its origin: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16).

pos: n. (Christopher Froschauer, c. 1490–1564, printer of Zurich)
etymology: Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; German Froschauer, from a Bavarian place-name, frog meadow.
biblical_def: Christopher Froschauer was Zwingli's printer and the press of the Zurich Reformation. In March 1522 he served sausages to a company that included Zwingli during Lent, and the ensuing uproar — the affair of the sausages — is conventionally where the Swiss Reformation begins; Froschauer's defence was that his workmen were exhausted from printing the epistles of Paul and needed feeding. He printed Zwingli's works, Bullinger's, the first Zurich Bible of 1531 — a complete German Bible five years ahead of Luther's finished version, translated by the Zurich ministers — and some nine hundred titles in all. The Froschauer Bibles were well made and cheap enough to sell, and they went into Anabaptist as well as Reformed households; the Swiss Brethren carried them to America. A press is a pulpit with a longer reach and no congregation of its own. “And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans” (Col 4:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Lent as the quadragesimal fast, and abstinence as the refraining from an indulgence of appetite.
webster_full: LENT, n. The quadragesimal fast, or a fast of forty days, observed by the christian church before Easter.
AB'STINENCE, n. The act or practice of voluntarily refraining from any action; particularly, the refraining from an indulgence of appetite.
IM'PRINT, n. The name of the printer and the place and date of publication, printed in a book.
QUAR'TO, n. A book of the size of the fourth of a sheet; a size made by twice folding a sheet.
scriptures: Col 4:16
And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.
Col 2:16
Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:
For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.
For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:
corruption_summary: Zwingli's printer, the affair of the sausages, and the Zurich Bible of 1531.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the retelling of the Lenten sausages as a piece of coarse provocation, a stunt that happened to start a reformation. The point at issue was precise and the participants knew it: whether the church may bind the conscience with a rule about food that Scripture does not impose. Froschauer's men had been working long hours on the epistles of Paul, which is where the answer is.

The principle to recover is that the apostle forbids exactly this kind of binding, by name and by category. “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days” (Col 2:16). The reason is that the kingdom does not consist in such things: “For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost” (Rom 14:17). And the creature is cleared with one condition attached: “if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4).

pos: n. (Hans Lufft, 1495–1584, printer of Wittenberg and of Luther's German Bible)
etymology: German Hans, a short form of Johannes, the LORD is gracious; Lufft, air, from Middle High German luft.
biblical_def: Hans Lufft printed the German Bible. He set up at Wittenberg about 1523 and in 1534 brought out the first complete Luther Bible, the whole canon in German from the original tongues, and over the next forty years his house produced something near a hundred thousand copies of it. The figure is almost unbelievable for the sixteenth century and it is roughly what the sources support. He was called the Bible-printer in his own lifetime. He printed with care: Luther, Melanchthon and others sat as a revision committee through the 1530s and 1540s and Lufft set their corrections edition by edition, so that the text improved steadily rather than drifting. He became a prosperous man and burgomaster of Wittenberg. What a hundred thousand German Bibles did to a nation over forty years is not measurable by any method we have, and it is the largest single fact about the German Reformation after Luther himself. “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impression as the copies of a book printed at one time, and revision as a re-examination for correction.
webster_full: IMPRES'SION, n. The copies of a book printed at one time; an edition.
REVI'SION, n. The act of reviewing; review; re-examination for correction.
CIRCULA'TION, n. The extent to which anything is diffused or spread abroad.
BUR'GOMASTER, n. The chief magistrate of a municipal town in Holland, Flanders and Germany.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field:
Another parable spake he unto them; The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.
corruption_summary: A hundred thousand German Bibles out of one Wittenberg house in forty years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the measuring of a reformation by its controversies, so that the pamphlet war and the diets fill the account and the quiet arithmetic of a press running for forty years is a footnote. Lufft's hundred thousand Bibles reached more German households than every polemical tract of the century put together, and they went on working after the controversies were cold.

The principle to recover is that the word works by its own nature and over time, which is why the Lord compares the kingdom to seed and to leaven rather than to a battle. “The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened” (Mat 13:33). The guarantee attached to the sending is unconditional: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).

etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Greek oporinos, of the late summer, a grecising of the surname Herbster.
biblical_def: Johann Oporinus was a professor of Greek who gave up the chair for a press and printed, in a working life of thirty years, some of the most consequential and most dangerous books of the century. He produced Vesalius's anatomy of 1543, the most beautiful scientific book of the age; he printed the first Latin translation of the Koran in 1543 and was briefly imprisoned by the Basel council for it until Luther and others argued that the best answer to a false religion is to let men read its book; and he printed the Magdeburg Centuries, the enormous Lutheran church history. He died poor, as scholarly printers generally did, having spent his returns on the next book. His career states the case for the free circulation of a dangerous text better than any argument: a man who thinks a false religion is false should want its book available, because error is refuted by examination and protected by prohibition. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines suppress as to keep in, to stifle, to conceal, and prove as to try, to ascertain by testing.
webster_full: SUPPRESS', v. To keep in; to restrain from utterance or vent; to stifle; to conceal.
PROVE, v. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality or truth by an experiment, or by a test.
ANAT'OMY, n. The art of dissecting or artificially separating the different parts of an animal body.
CEN'SOR, n. An officer whose business was to inspect the manners of the people; one who examines books before publication.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Eph 5:13
But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light.
corruption_summary: The Basel printer briefly jailed for the Latin Koran, and freed because Luther argued for it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs in two directions and the sixteenth century saw both. One says that a dangerous book should be suppressed because the simple will be harmed by it, which assumes the error is stronger than the truth and keeps the faithful permanently unable to answer what they have never read. The other says that nothing is dangerous, which is not what Scripture says either: John tells a church that many false prophets have gone out into the world.

The principle to recover is that the believer is commanded to test rather than either to swallow or to avoid. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21) is two imperatives and the first is examination. John gives the same instruction with the reason attached: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1). And error is dealt with by exposure rather than burial: “all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light” (Eph 5:13).

pos: n. (Christopher Plantin, c. 1520–1589, printer of Antwerp)
etymology: Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; French Plantin, from plante, a plant, a shoot.
biblical_def: Christopher Plantin was a Frenchman who settled at Antwerp, became the greatest printer in Europe, and at his height ran sixteen presses. He printed the Antwerp Polyglot for Philip II, liturgical books for Spain in enormous quantities under a royal monopoly, and a steady stream of scholarship; his house still stands in Antwerp as a museum with the shop, the types and the ledgers intact, which is why more is known about his business than about any other printer of the century. His religious position was ambiguous and probably deliberately so: he was associated with the Family of Love, a quietist sect, while printing for the Spanish crown and employing Protestant correctors. He survived the Spanish Fury and the sack of Antwerp and kept the business through it. That ambiguity was good for the press and is not a model. A trade that required a man to be legible to everyone and committed to no one is a trade that tests the conscience hard. “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines monopoly as the sole power of vending any species of goods, and neutrality as a state of indifference, taking no part on either side.
webster_full: MONOP'OLY, n. The sole power of vending any species of goods, obtained by engrossing the articles in market or by a license from government.
NEUTRAL'ITY, n. A state of indifference; the state of a nation that takes no part in a contest between others.
CORRECT'OR, n. One who corrects; one who revises a writing or the proofs of a book.
FOUNT, n. In printing, a complete set of types of one size, with all that is necessary for printing.
scriptures: Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
Rev 3:15
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.

Jam 1:8

corruption_summary: Sixteen presses at Antwerp, a royal monopoly, and a religion nobody could pin down.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the admiration of the survivor, which reads Plantin's ambiguity as a prudent accommodation in an impossible position and leaves it there. The position was genuinely impossible: Antwerp changed hands repeatedly, printers were executed for the wrong book, and a man with sixteen presses and a workforce had a great deal to lose. The explanation is real and it is not an exoneration.

The principle to recover is that Scripture does not recognise a permanent middle position in this matter and says so in the sharpest words it has. “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24). The risen Lord's word to Laodicea is harder still and prefers either extreme to the middle: “I would thou wert cold or hot” (Rev 3:15). James gives the diagnosis in seven words: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jam 1:8).

pos: n. (Richard Grafton, c. 1511–1573, London printer of the English Bible)
etymology: Germanic Richard, strong in rule; English Grafton, from a place-name, the grove farm.
biblical_def: Richard Grafton was a London grocer who, with Edward Whitchurch, paid for and arranged the printing of the Matthew Bible of 1537 and then the Great Bible of 1539, the first English Bible authorised to be set up in every parish church in the kingdom. The Great Bible was begun in Paris because the French presses were better, and when the Inquisition seized the sheets Grafton and Coverdale recovered what they could, bought back a quantity of the printed paper that had been sold off as waste to a haberdasher, brought presses and workmen across to London, and finished it there. He became king's printer under Edward VI, printed the Book of Common Prayer, and then printed the proclamation of Lady Jane Grey's accession, which cost him the patent and his liberty for a while under Mary. He wrote chronicles in his later years. The man risked his money and his neck on English Bibles and got nine days of the wrong queen. “So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).

webster_full: PAT'ENT, n. A writ or instrument granting to a person the exclusive right or privilege of making or selling a thing.

corruption_summary: The grocer who bought back his seized Bible from a haberdasher and finished it in London.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that the English Bible arrived by royal decision, since the Great Bible was set up in the churches by authority. The authority came late and was never reliable. The money, the risk and the recovery of the seized Paris sheets were a grocer's and a haberdasher's business, and the same crown that authorised the book in 1539 jailed its printer in 1553.

The principle to recover is that Scripture records this exact sequence once already and makes a point of it. Jehoiakim burned the roll and the word was written again with additions: “who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words” (Jer 36:32). Gamaliel states the rule the Inquisition at Paris had not grasped: “if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it” (Act 5:39).

pos: n. (Edward Whitchurch, d. 1562, London printer, partner in the Great Bible)
etymology: Old English Eadweard, rich guardian; English Whitchurch, from a place-name, the white church.
biblical_def: Edward Whitchurch was Grafton's partner and the quieter half of the pair that put the English Bible into the parish churches. He was a London merchant who financed the Matthew Bible of 1537 and the Great Bible of 1539, shared the royal patent for the service books under Edward VI, and printed the Book of Common Prayer and the first Book of Homilies — the set sermons appointed to be read in churches where the minister could not preach, which is a sober acknowledgment of how few English clergy in 1547 could preach at all. Under Mary he fled abroad; under Elizabeth he returned, and he married Cranmer's widow. His partnership with Grafton is the ordinary shape of the whole business: these books were brought into existence by laymen with capital who took a commercial and a physical risk, not by clergy with a plan. “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people” (2Ch 17:9).

Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
Act 8:30
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
corruption_summary: The merchant who paid for the Great Bible and printed the Homilies for clergy who could not preach.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern contempt for the Book of Homilies as a device for muzzling the clergy, a set text imposed where free preaching should have been. The reason for it was practical and humiliating and the Edwardian church did not hide it: a great many parish incumbents in 1547 were incapable of preaching a sound sermon, and the choice was between a read homily and nothing.

The principle to recover is that hearing is the ordinary means and that a church must supply it somehow. “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) states the necessity; a homily read aloud is a poor second and is not nothing. The permanent remedy is the one Paul prescribes to a minister: “Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13), which is a programme for making preachers rather than for replacing them.

pos: n. (Thomas Vautrollier, d. 1587, Huguenot printer in London and Edinburgh)
etymology: Greek Thomas, from Aramaic teoma, a twin; French Vautrollier, from a surname of the Troyes region.
biblical_def: Thomas Vautrollier was a Huguenot refugee who set up a press in Blackfriars in London and became one of the best printers in England — his Latin and Greek work was good enough that the scholars preferred him. He printed Calvin's Institutes in Thomas Norton's English, Beza's New Testament, Luther on Galatians, and a quantity of music. In 1584 he got into trouble over a book and went to Edinburgh, where he printed for two years and gave Scotland a standard of typography it had not had; the Scottish printers who came after him learned from his work. He came back to London and died there. His apprentice Richard Field married his widow, took over the house, and printed Shakespeare's first poems from it. The thread is worth noticing: a French refugee from the massacres sets up a press in London, prints Calvin into English, trains a Stratford boy, and the house that printed Beza's New Testament printed the first English poetry of the age. “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines refugee as one who flies to a shelter or place of safety, and apprentice as one bound to another to learn a trade.
webster_full: REF'UGEE, n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who in times of persecution flees to a foreign country for safety.
APPREN'TICE, n. One who is bound by covenant to serve a mechanic or other person for a certain time, with a view to learn his art or trade.
TYPOG'RAPHY, n. The art of printing; the operation of impressing letters on paper.
DEN'IZEN, n. A stranger admitted to residence and certain rights in a foreign country.
scriptures: Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
corruption_summary: The Huguenot refugee whose London press printed Calvin into English and trained Shakespeare's printer.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the accounting of refugees purely as a cost, which was argued in Elizabethan London as loudly as anywhere and was answered by the evidence. The French and Dutch Protestant refugees brought the silk weaving, the printing, the glass and a dozen other trades, and the country that received them was richer in skill within a generation. That is not the reason to receive the persecuted, but it is a standing rebuke to the arithmetic that says otherwise.

The principle to recover is that the law of Moses settles the question of the resident stranger with a command and a memory attached. “But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Lev 19:34). The New Testament keeps it as a standing duty: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2), and the Lord puts it in the judgment scene: “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35).

pos: n. (John Day, 1522–1584, London printer of Foxe's Acts and Monuments)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Day, from Old English daeg, a byname.
biblical_def: John Day was the best-equipped printer in Elizabethan England and the publisher of the book that shaped English Protestant self-understanding for three centuries. He printed Foxe's Acts and Monuments in 1563 and in four further editions, each enormous, each heavily illustrated with woodcuts of the burnings, each a commercial undertaking of a size no other English printer could have attempted. He also printed Tyndale's and Frith's works, the first English church music books, and the first book printed in Anglo-Saxon types, which he had cut so that Archbishop Parker could publish the Old English homilies and show that the medieval English church had not always taught what Rome now taught. Day was imprisoned under Mary and had to print secretly under a false imprint. His woodcuts are the reason the Marian burnings are visible to the English imagination at all. “Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light” (Luk 12:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines woodcut as an engraving on wood, and imprint as the name of the printer with the place and date of publication.
webster_full: WOOD'CUT, n. An engraving on wood, or a print from such an engraving.
IM'PRINT, n. The name of the printer, with the place and date of publication, printed in a book.
EN'GRAVING, n. The act or art of cutting figures or letters on hard substances; a print from an engraved block.
SAX'ON, a. Pertaining to the Saxons or to their language.
scriptures: Luk 12:3
Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops.
Luk 12:2
For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.
Eph 5:13
But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
corruption_summary: The press behind Foxe's book, and the woodcuts that fixed the Marian fires in English memory.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the dismissal of Foxe as propaganda, which is an easy charge and a lazy one. The book has faults: it is partisan, it is credulous in places, and Foxe sometimes prints what he was told. It also quotes documents at enormous length, including the registers of the bishops who conducted the trials, and modern scholarship checking those citations has generally found them sound. A book may be an advocate's and still be a record.

The principle to recover is that God has arranged for things done in private to become public, and that the church's keeping of such records is a participation in that arrangement rather than a vindictiveness. “For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known” (Luk 12:2). The exposure is described as the work of light: “all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light” (Eph 5:13). And the slain are already counted under the altar (Rev 6:9); a printer only makes the count legible.
